items.title: Ordinal Bounty #0: 100,000 sats for a single sat whose ordinal ends with a 0
items.text:
Ordinal numbers are serial numbers for satoshis. In an effort get people interested, I've been offering bounties on specific ordinals, or ordinals with specific qualities. I had a huge grab bag of bounties, but I decided to change it up and focus on one bounty at a time.

The current bounty is [here](https://ordinals.com/bounties)!

To claim the bounty, send a single sat* to the address on the bounty page. The catch: The sat must be the first sat in the output you send. This is stipulated because otherwise, sending at least 10 contiguous sats would be sufficient to claim the bounty, and that would be too easy.

To claim the bounty, you'll have to understand [how ordinals work](https://github.com/casey/ord/blob/master/bip.mediawiki), look up some ordinals you own on the [ordinals.com block explorer](ordinals.com) and write some pretty simple code to construct a transaction with input sand outputs in the right order.

NB Whenever you look up a utxo you own on a block explorer, it's a privacy leak! You can run your own copy of the block explorer, get the code [on github](https://github.com/casey/ord).

The reward is 100,000 sats**.

The bounty can only be claimed once, and is definitely unclaimed as long as no transactions have been sent to the bounty address.

The bounty page contains instructions on how to claim the bounty.

If anyone claims this bounty, I'll come up with another, harder one. Maybe one day the bounty will be to find one of the [three](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′336″0‴) [epic](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′672″0‴) [ordinals](https://ordinals.com/ordinal/0°0′1008″0‴) mined so far.

\* In practice you'll have to send more, so your transaction doesn't have dust outputs, and thus be non-standard and not relayed.

items.title: Resolvr: a Bounty Marketplace that takes the Agent out of Escrow
items.text:
Recently, a popular bounty marketplace, BountySource, [stopped paying out bounties](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1586) to developers. Many users reported outstanding or significantly delayed payouts.  [[1](https://github.com/bountysource/core/issues/1539)] [[2](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900)]. The entities or persons running BountySource likely misused the escrowed funds being held for bounties.  Bounty posters and developers have been searching for an alternative. 

But the risk of exit scams or insolvency are inherent to all centralzied escrow agent.  That's why most jurisdictions place onerous fiduciary duties on escrow agents to faithfully hold funds for safekeeping and deliver them according to the terms of the deal.   But it can take time and money to get compensation through the courts and usually recovery is for pennies on the dollar. The costs of legal action outweighs any bounty amounts lost through embezzlement.   

So some existing platforms, like Algora, don't bother with escrow.  But, as one former BountySource user [pointed out](https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/issues/5900#issuecomment-1771603383), that just shifts the trust to the bounty grantor.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/65395e3087238f2bcef5379f/9d1297aa-6072-41b9-bea3-a57814b2dee1/more+trust+in+donor.png?content-type=image%2Fpng)

Replit provides a bounty marketplace that does escrow bounty funds, but payouts are not instant or free.  Users are awarded Replit's token (cycles) for solving bounties, and must request payout in USD by email.  Users are charged a 25% withdrawal fee for any bounty funds earned, and there is a minimum withdrawal amount of $350. So, not only are you trusting that Replit won't go bankrupt, you are paying through the nose for that risk. 

[Resolvr](https://www.resolvr.io) takes the centralized agent out of escrow.  It doesn't control or possesses the bounty funds.  Instead, Resolvr leverages bitcoin's native programmability to attest to whether the bounty has been solved, triggering payout automatically.  This removes the need to trust the platform or grantor.

And Resolvr doesn't decide whether the bounty has been solved;  a panel of crowdsourced developers performs the review.   

Resolvr is the first bounty marketplace to offer dependable escrow and payouts, as well as transparent dispute resolution.  Oh, and it's cheaper than the existing alternatives.

You can [sign up](https://www.resolvr.io/) to be an alpha tester today! And check out the [GitHub](https://github.com/Resolvr-io) and join the conversation on [discord](https://discord.gg/DsqRw8My4m).

Get your bounties ready!

items.title: Intel Ends Its $100,000 Bug Bounty Program
items.text: Intel has officially suspended its Bug Bounty Program, which offered security researchers compensation for finding and reporting security vulnerabilities. The program is now marked as suspended on the Intigriti platform, but Intel has not provided a detailed explanation for this decision. Previously, Intel organized a series of bounties for those discovering bugs and vulnerabilities, divided into four tiers. In tier one, the highest payout was $5,000; tier two offered $10,000; tier three provided $30,000; and the most severe bugs in tier four could be compensated with $100,000. Tier four was intended for major vulnerability disclosures, like Spectre or Meltdown, which were significant security issues a few years ago.

items.title: Reflecting a bit on The Zap Wars
items.text:
We've been [talking about downzapping](https://stacker.news/search?q=downzapping&what=posts) a bunch. Obviously, the rewards are absolutely, wild with some stackers receiving 6-figure payouts. The discussion on the most recent [SNL](https://stacker.news/items/1568942/r/Undisciplined) reminded me that I wanted to write up some of my thoughts about this situation.

I wrote about [Incentivizing Downzapping](https://stacker.news/items/621288/r/Undisciplined) and how [Punishment is a Public Good](https://stacker.news/items/619793/r/Undisciplined) a couple of years ago. Check those out for background to my thoughts here.

# Are the incentives broken?

A prevailing sentiment seems to be that the incentives on SN are not working to curate content (and maybe they aren't). We should be cautious about overreacting to the actions of a particular bad actor, especially in the short term, though.

We're seeing general SN activity increasing ([zaps, unique stackers, item creation](https://stacker.news/stackers/all/month)), as the boosting vs downzapping battle rages. This is part of the mechanics of the site and it's at least directionally having the self-correcting effect we hope to see. More users making good content, supported by more zapping, makes boosting stuff to the top more costly for scammers and, more importantly, is exactly what we want for SN.

I've lived through a few other periods of fervor about the incentives being broken, usually ignited by a particular bad actor seemingly getting away with something. I urged caution and patience in those episodes too and in short order the self-correcting mechanisms we have in place did seem to kick in.

Ultimately, though, incentives drive outcomes by affecting aggregate behavior, not necessarily each individual's. Any given individual can have utterly bizarre preferences and with sufficient resources they can do undesirable things.

If we think the incentives have mostly been working to curate content well, then we should let this situation breath and see how it develops. Hemorrhaging sats to promote your scam to people who are wise to it is not sustainable behavior and unsustainable behaviors burn themselves out.

# Are direct confrontations the solution?

Another aspect I've been thinking about is whether getting into a Downzap War is even the strategically correct move. The natural half-life on visibility from boost and zap decay is a powerful mechanism, especially for those of us with supposedly low time-preference.

Might this scammer have passed silently into the night, if not engaged in a big battle for visibility? Once egos get involved, behaviors can become extreme and entrenched.

What if, instead of directly challenging offending posts through a downzap confrontation, territory owners put their new ([arguably ill-gotten and undeserved](https://stacker.news/items/1563313/r/Undisciplined)) revenue towards boosting the good content on SN?

# Punishers go hard

Something I didn't mention in [my post about punishment](https://stacker.news/items/619793/r/Undisciplined) is that once someone decides to engage in punishment, they are often willing to expend quite a lot of resources on it. We're seeing that now with enormous downzaps that are well beyond what we see zapped towards good content.

# What's curation worth to you?

It's sort of odd that punishers are willing to spend more on punishment than they are on support. It's all just curation, after all. Moving someone down 10 spots is the same as moving those 10 people up 1 spot, except that the sats go out community wide instead of to the producers of the better content.

What I think is being revealed by very large downzapping is that some people value the curation of the front page of SN far beyond what they've been putting towards zaps. I've been banging on about this forever (just scroll through [my top discussion posts](https://stacker.news/Undisciplined/discussions?by=sats)), but it still seems to me like stackers haven't internalized the rational self-interest value of zapping the content they like.

For your own sake, zap big and zap often.

***

# How to do wanted posters

@Car pitched the idea of wanted posters as a mechanism for flagging scammy bullshit but didn't offer @k00b any real way of implementing them in a fashion that is emergent from the community.

This is a place where I think relying on our global trust scores is valuable. Any post that's underwater with trust-weighted, time-discounted zaps vs downzaps could be tagged with a wanted poster to alert readers of SN that the upstanding members of this community think caution is warranted with those posts.

***

**TL;DR**
Stacker News has an impressive array of self-correcting mechanisms, but they are not instantaneous. Think about what you want SN to be and whether you're already doing what you think you should towards that end, before pushing to change the rules.

I very much look forward to a lively discussion about this.

items.title: [Book Review] Colonialism: A Moral Reckoning
items.text:
**Review of *Colonialism: A Moral Reckoning*, by Nigel Biggar**

![](https://www.harpercollins.com/cdn/shop/files/9780008511630_1808b77c-2914-4b37-aee1-3acd4156a4a5.jpg?v=1720130295&width=350)

## The strange inconsistency of the modern left

Observe Western politics long enough and you'll inevitably come across the strange inconsistency of the modern left.  This strange inconsistency is perhaps no better illustrated than in the phrase "Queers for Palestine"---because why does it make sense for queers to support a culture that's explicitly hostile to them, and even if they support Palestinian rights, why does it make sense to them to attach queer identity to that support?

Observe Western politics for some time longer and you may eventually conclude that the unifying theme of the modern left is *anti-colonialism*.  That the primary project of the modern left is to erase all vestiges of influence from the time of European and Christian cultural dominance.   This theory of the left, I believe, carries much more explanatory power than other theories.  For example, some people say that the left is  concerned primarily with liberating the oppressed.  But if the left cared primarily about oppressor/oppressed relationships, then why do they not speak up about Chinese oppression of Uighurs, or Nigerian oppression of Christians?  Categories of oppression only seem to matter when it is Western culture doing the oppression.  So the unifying theme that best explains the modern left is not anti-oppression, but anti-colonialism.

## One can see why anti-colonialism is attractive

And one can see why anti-colonialism would be an attractive ideology. From a purely empirical perspective, it's hard to deny that the advantaged position of certain demographic groups derive at least in part from historical European Christian hegemony. It is also impossible to deny that Western cultural imperialism gave rise to many human rights abuses suffered by non-Westerners at the hands of Westerners. Introspection is always and everywhere a virtue, so for the Westerner, it makes good sense to introspect about past wrongs and to apologize for them. For the non-Westerner, such introspection may be encouraged as a means to either achieve reconciliation or to garner material concessions.

## What's missing is the relevant counterfactual

But what's missing from the anti-colonial impulse is an assessment of the relevant counterfactual.  Yes, Western colonialism led to abuses. But what *other* abuses, and how many and to what degree, would have happened had the Europeans not engaged in their colonial past?  Can we fairly say that the world have been better had the Europeans not engaged in their colonial past?  By what measure do we judge the result of Western imperialism versus the cultures that they displaced?

## A fair look at the spectrum of humanity involved

Nigel Biggar tackles these questions in *Colonialism: A Moral Reckoning*.  A moral philosopher, (like Adam Smith),  Nigel Biggar is interested in telling the moral history of European colonialism, with a fair look at the entire spectrum of the humanity involved: from the European nobles who made policy from afar, to the lowly settler engaged in conflict with the natives, to the natives with varied attitudes towards European colonization, to the modern academics who look back at these stories through agenda-tinted lenses.

## A much needed corrective to anti-colonial tropes

The book is a much needed corrective to modern anti-colonial tropes. Biggar does not shy away from acknowledging some of the horrors that resulted from European colonization, but he rightly points out that European colonization did much good around the world too. For example, he points out the British bore as much economist cost in trying to abolish slavery around the world as it profited from the slave trade prior to abolition.  He also demonstrates, through primary sources, the wide extent to which many Europeans were motivated by genuine humanitarian sentiments.

Most importantly, he highlights the messy nature of human morality, showing us that it doesn't make sense to paint *any* culture with too broad of a brush, Western or otherwise. Within the European colonizers there were both saints and sinners, abolitionists and slavers, and the whole spectrum of humanity; just so amongst the native populations as well. Among the natives there were those who would have enslaved each other were it not for the European abolitionists, and there were others who welcomed European traditions as a relief against their oppressive native traditions. The picture that Biggar paints is simply one of *messiness*: when two cultures come into contact with each other, stuff happens; often, every kind of stuff you can imagine.

## Least sympathetic group: modern academics

Perhaps the group that comes across least sympathetic in Biggar's analysis is the modern left leaning academic. Biggar shows that much of modern scholarship is biased and agenda driven. He does this by showing examples of modern academics taking historical quotes out of context so that they can paint a more damning picture of European attitudes than is deserved. Biggar instead shows that European attitudes were varied and diverse, and that claims about European racism are often unfair and overstated.

## Book contains a plethora of historical quotations

The most useful aspect of the book is its plethora of historical quotations that show a varied range of both European and native attitudes. The book forcefully makes the point that many Europeans truly were motivated by altruistic goals of bettering the lives of natives; and crucially that many natives also welcomed their efforts. But he also highlights how settlers and natives sometimes came into conflict, and how differences in tradition often led to social frictions which made it difficult for Europeans and natives to truly integrate, even if the desire was there.

Below, I have picked out a few select quotes for a few specific topics.

***

## On slavery

*On the degree to which the British were instrumental in fighting slavery worldwide*

> The humanitarian motive to suppress the slave trade and slavery remained a common reason for imperial endeavour in Africa from the late nineteenth century into the twentieth. It caused the British government to lean upon the khedive of Egypt to sign the Anglo-Egyptian Slave Trade Convention in 1877. It propelled General Charles Gordon into the Sudan in the same year. It found expression in the principles of the Imperial British East Africa Company, when it was founded in 1888. It featured among the reasons for establishing a British protectorate in Nyasaland in 1891. And it was one reason for the invasion of the Sokoto Caliphate (now northern Nigeria) by Frederick Lugard in 1903.

...

> Moreover in absolute terms the British spent almost as much attempting to suppress the trade in the forty-seven years, 1816–62, as they received in profits over the same length of time leading up to 1807. And by any more reasonable assessment of profits and direct costs, the nineteenth-century costs of suppression were certainly bigger than the eighteenth-century benefits.

...

> Basil Cave, who was consul-general in Zanzibar when domestic slavery was finally abolished in 1909, bore witness to this when he reflected with satisfaction on the local history of British efforts at abolition: "All the time British influence was being steadily brought to bear upon the Sultan. Whenever an opportunity presented itself, when the Sultan appealed for political, financial, or personal assistance, when some benefit was offered or conferred, occasion was always taken to introduce some fresh anti-slavery measure and to move one more step forward towards final abolition. As a result, the whole of the servile population of East Africa has been freed from bondage without a hand, and almost without a voice, being raised in protest."

***

## On racial attitudes

*On the degree to which racism wasn't isolated to Europeans, and how some natives welcomed European cultural change*

> And in the 1940s, Gerald Hanley, then an officer in the British Army, found Somalis unshakeable in their prejudice against other black peoples: "I had once tried hard to get the Somalis to give up their contempt for Bantu people. But 'We cannot obey slaves', Somalis told me. 'It is impossible for us to live under slave people even when they are in British uniform and have arms.' I could not change the memory they \[the Somalis] had of a time when these Bantu people were slave material for the Muslim world to the north. That was the trouble, the curse of race, looks, noses, lips, eyes, legends. Colour has little to do with it."

...

> Looking back on the period 1890–1904, Baba of Karo, a Muslim African woman in what is now Nigeria, had this to say: "We Habe wanted them \[the Europeans] to come, it was the Fulani who did not like it. When the Europeans came the Habe saw that if you worked for them they paid you for it, they didn't say, like the Fulani, 'Commoner, give me this! Commoner, bring me that!' The Europeans said that there were to be no more slaves; if someone said 'Slave!' you could complain to the alkali who would punish the master who said it.  No one used the word 'slave' any more.  In the old days if the chief liked the look of your daughter he would take her and put her in his house; you could do nothing about it. Now they don’t do that."

...

> Far from being reluctant converts, many Africans were attracted to Christianity as a source of liberation. Writing in 1959, Ndabaningi Sithole asserted that "one of the unique teachings of the Bible, especially the New Testament, is the worth and dignity of the individual in the sight of God. The Bible is redeeming the African individual from the power of superstition, individuality-crushing tradition, witchcraft, and other forces that do not make for progress. The Bible-liberated African is now reasserting himself not only over tribal but also over colonial authority, since these two are fundamentally the same."

***

## On assimilation and "cultural genocide"

*Regarding the controversy over residential schools in Canada*

> However, the instrument of assimilation that now attracts the fiercest opprobrium was Canada's system of residential schools. The motivation for establishing these schools was basically humanitarian, namely, to enable pupils to adapt and survive in a world that was changing radically. This was a general need that many native people themselves acknowledged, as they found themselves unable to sustain their traditional hunting-and-gathering economy. As Chief Paulus Claus of the Bay of Quinte Mohawk said at the July 1846 conference at Orillia (in what is now southern Ontario), "we cannot be a people unless we conform ourselves to the ways of the white man". Consequently, native leaders actively lobbied missionaries to set up schools that would teach their children agricultural skills, English language and Christian religion.

...

> Quite how extensive the \[school] failings were is difficult to determine. Certainly, they were not universal. In 1886, for example, Red Crow, a powerful chief in the Blood nation of the Blackfoot Confederacy, together with several of his fellow chiefs, "had been greatly impressed by the attainment of Indian youths at the Anglican Mohawk Institute". Moreover, had there not been a significant record of success, "numerous Indian groups" would not have lobbied, as they did, for the establishment of residential schools well into the twentieth century

...

> As for first-hand testimony, it is equivocal. As J.R. Miller, author of the standard history of the residential schools, has commented: "While there are many former students who testify to the damage that the suppression of their language and other things did to them and to people they knew, there are also former students who firmly deny that their school experience scarred them or their fellow students. Too many ex-pupils have spoken positively of the experience as a whole, or of particular school workers who befriended them, or even of the balance of positive consequences that they struck after weighing both sides to justify ignoring or downplaying such memories. Too many argue that the schools were important sources of knowledge and preparation for them to trivialize all positive recollections as the products of individual peculiarities."

***

## Conclusion

To conclude, I'd recommend this book to anyone interested in understanding European colonial history and anyone who is looking for a corrective to modern anti-colonialist sentiments.

items.title: Should we want to grow Stacker News? If so, how?
items.text:
I admit that I have issues with insecurity. I'm constantly afraid that things that I like will go away, and that is a fear has been re-enforced over the years with the great things that we've all lost. This anxiety applies to Stacker News as well and I've had the lifelong conviction that if you aren't growing, you're dying; a quote that I heard my dad shout from a pulpit of our church when I was twelve or thirteen. I still hear that line in the back of my head when I look at communitites that I've become a part of.

I like SN. It's one of the few places on the internet that has a good incentive structure and on top of that, an incentive structure that ties into bitcoin. I haven't been here long and I'm also pretty late to the party so my long-term experience isn't really there. I'm sure that there's a lot that I've missed because of that. Regardless, I feel a connection to this place and want it to succeed. 

A part of that desire to see this place succeed is growth. If I could, I would want to see a million people here, zapping around and arguing but that isn't necessarily a good thing. Places lose part of what made them great when huge crowds show up. Generally speaking, the more people who show up, the lower the average quality. That million people might just be the worst thing that could happen here compared to a tiny trickle of new users or even losing users. I can understand why someone would want this place to stay small.

Would that happen here? Would seeing huge growth across Stacker News ruin it? If not, how do we grow? If the path ahead for this place is growth, how do we ensure the people that we draw here are the kind of people we would want to bring in? I know this is a bit odd for someone who hasn't managed to be here for a full year, but this really does bother me.

items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/158419)

I’ve put together a [catalogue](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks) and a corresponding [post](https://deadmanoz.xyz/posts/2026/invalid-blocks) detailing 143 Bitcoin blocks that met the required proof-of-work target but failed a consensus rule, from the 2010 overflow to two previously unreported F2Pool timestamp failures from 2026!!

The catalogue brings together the surviving evidence for each case, so anyone can independently verify which consensus rule the block broke.

A few findings:

* **The two F2Pool headers from April and July this year have timestamps roughly 7 and 14 days below their parents’ median time past.** Both were found in merge-mined auxiliary chains; neither has a known Bitcoin-side capture.
* **Auxiliary chains preserve 49 of the 143 headers**, and provide the catalogue’s only recorded observation for 35. They check their own rules, so they can preserve evidence of candidates that Bitcoin peers reject.
* **89 blocks contain the same P2SH-invalid transaction**, mined between April and July 2012. Archived transaction lists and preserved headers establish its inclusion in each.
* **127 of the 143 have no complete body.** The surviving headers, coinbases or transaction inclusion proofs, together with chain context, still establish the failures.
* Another 10 reported cases remain separate because the evidence is insufficient.

The same merge mining research also recovered roughly 1,400 stale headers new to the [stale-blocks collection](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/stale-blocks). Merge mining has proved to be a productive side channel for both stales and invalids, and monitoring those chains is essential to a holistic Bitcoin monitoring effort.

In my [merge mining monitor](https://mmm.deadmanoz.xyz/) tool you can step through all invalid-blocks discovered in the merge-mined record (note that invalid blocks are currently called error blocks, this was the language I originally used):

![](https://m.stacker.news/158420)

If you have old node files, pool logs or other records that could fill a gap, contributions and corrections are very welcome.

[https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/invalid-blocks)

items.title: Neptune’s Brood: The First Bitcoin Novel
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/156420)


I can’t believe I never heard of [Neptune’s Brood](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/71956901) until last week. In my defense, I am not much of a sci fi reader, nor have I ever heard of it mentioned in any bitcoin podcast, conference, article or on any social media site. 

The author, Charles Stross, is a fairly well known science fiction writer. The book, part of the Freyaverse series, was shortlisted for the Hugo Award for Best Science Fiction/Fantasy Novel of 2014. I discovered that Nobel Prize Winner and Widely Recognized Douchebag Paul Krugman really [liked](https://archive.nytimes.com/krugman.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/05/20/the-theory-of-interstellar-finance/) Stross’s treatment of “interstellar finance.” This fact alone almost caused me to dismiss “Neptune’s Brood”, but curiosity got the best of me.

So why is this book so obscure? Most people I know who are obsessed with bitcoin are also obsessed with science fiction. Even more incredibly, it has the distinction of being the first novel in history to mention bitcoin. That’s what my research tells me, and I stand by that assertion until I’m proven wrong. Start hunting.

Full disclosure – I have not read the book, so I am not calling this post a book review. However, I did read a lot about the book, and my copy is in the mail. From what I have learned, bitcoin is not just mentioned, but it is critical to the plot.

The novel opens with a quote from David Graeber’s book, [Debt: The First 5,000 Years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt:_The_First_5,000_Years). I did read that book, and while I enjoyed it and learned a lot, I didn’t generally buy his debt over barter theory thesis.

Regarding the plot, I have seen it described as a financial sci fi novel. Set in the future, bitcoin forms the basis for an interstellar financial system because it is theft-proof. Each coin is cryptographically signed by the mind of its owner.

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune's_Brood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune's_Brood)

Although I don’t know the details, money is broken up into three types:

> Fast money is ordinary day-to-day cash, medium money covers investment instruments within a single planetary system, and slow money is reserved for interstellar investment that takes centuries or millennia to mature, with slow-money transactions relying on a three-way cryptoverification scheme that trades at one-third the speed of light.

Some reviewers say the writing is too dense, and the author uses too many obscure words. It is also criticized for spending too much time lecturing about the “slow money” financial system rather than focusing on plot or character development. As bitcoiners we may have a greater tolerance for financial discussion.

Members of Bitcointalk mentioned the book back in 2013. TraderTimm posted on July 9, 2013, saying:

> in the novel's economy, essentially everyone is born into debt for the cost of the technology that constitutes them, large banks are linked by multi-light-year gigawatt laser beams, and there are cryptographic signing methods with bitcoin invoked as a nod to a system capable of underpinning entire civilizations.

He added that Stross, as a former programmer, would understand how [bitcoin] actually works.

Wladimir van der Laan, later bitcoin core’s lead maintainer, also recommended the book to programmers, along with Daniel Suarez’s Daemon" series.

Once I have my copy I will read it, and then maybe review it if someone doesn’t beat me to the punch.




[satwize]([https://satwize.com](https://satwize.com/)) will also be stocking it soon.

Some are simply goofy, like [this synth that is made to look like windows in the 90s](https://windowcandy.thealternativedesktopsynthesizer.garden/). It doesn't do anything particularly exciting, but you could bring a controller and a laptop to a gig, and it will function just fine.

Others may only work at home, [like this one](https://qwertytempered.thealternativedesktopsynthesizer.garden/), tempered to your keyboard.

![](https://m.stacker.news/156942)

Nevertheless, there are options to really create some new music with it. I like finding some good sounds, and then just typing the verbal thoughts in my head.

One is a [polyrhythmic drum machine](https://polymolly.thealternativedesktopsynthesizer.garden/) for DJs that are going for that filling-the-dancefloor-with-nerds sound.

Anyway, @SimpleStacker was out bot-bating last week and straight up blew my mind with [this post](https://stacker.news/items/1567486) on the Collatz Conjecture. Dude! I love learning about this kind of thing. It's kind of like the opposite of Conway's Game of Life. With this set of rules, you can start with infinite complexity and always end in the same simple sequence.

Anyway, through persistent badgering, I learned that he had made [this cool visualizer](https://henry-kung.github.io/collatz/) for it with his son, and I immediately wanted to **hear** it as well. So...I would like to share with you [Hailstone Harmonics](https://hailstoneharmonics.thealternativedesktopsynthesizer.garden/). It may not be the most functional herb in my garden, but you can definitely get some pretty sounds (the rhythms of the bass in particular) out of it.

items.title: Shitcoin/scam ads on SN - yay or nay, and why?
items.text:
*I just spent some time with @siggy47 in yesterday's saloon arguing about moral aspects around shitcoin posts on SN and the boosts that (in my opinion) make them into ads. I have a pretty strong opinion on this but since the intensity of my feelings don't make me right, I wonder what stackers think.*

### Premise 

The premise I'd pose is that **boosts are paid advertising**, very similar to how you'd pay FB or TikTok to make your post/video appear in more feeds, except on SN, you don't pay SN. Instead, you pay:

1. The territory owner(s) for 70% of the boost, and
2. Reward-eligible stackers for 30% of the boost

So basically, territory owners and stackers that get a piece of the daily rewards are getting paid for each boost. A boost that sits unchallenged is therefore an accepted advertisement: "We accept your sats, have your stage".

### Consequence for boosted shitcoin and scam posts

As long as my premise holds, when a shitcoiner posts a story about their new thing, or a scammer posts a new product that rugs its users, and boosts it, it too is an ad. Sold to the scammer/shitcoiner by the people that received the boost sats, and therefore, these stackers profit from the scam/shitcoin.

If a territory owner disagrees with the scam being promoted on their territory, then they can, at no additional cost, downzap the post for that 70%. These sats will then go 100% to rewards, making the remainder of undoing the boost, if they feel so inclined, sit in the hands of the stackers that will receive the payout. At this point, 100% of the boost will be paid out to stackers in the next rewards payout, and the scammer can be 100% neutralized, only if 30% of the stackers are in agreement that the scam should not be promoted. So stackers as a whole have the upper hand here.

Now of course, this means that you say good-bye to a portion of those nice little sats that you just got magically paid out to you for not doing anything other than zap here and there (hard work, I know.)

### Questions to the stackers

***Is it okay to profit from scammers? Would you use your "hard-earned" reward sats to reduce the visibility of scams? Or is opti being a delusional idealist? Or even an evil aspiring dictator?***

I hope we can talk about this.

items.title: Why Sat-Digital-Gold can't win without Nah•Sovereign•Diamond
items.text:
*"A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution... The cost of mediation increases transaction costs, limiting the minimum practical transaction size and cutting off the possibility for small casual transactions..."* — Satoshi Nakamoto

*"I wanted to pick a denomination that would make prices similar to existing currencies, but without knowing the future, that's very hard..."* — Satoshi Nakamoto

We did not engineer the Bitcoin timechain for institutional settlement or Wall Street portfolios. It was built to protect the individual from the theft of inflation. As the generation of builders continuing Satoshi Nakamoto's work, we realize that to fulfill this ultimate vision and shield the working class from the legacy fiat machine, we must solve the exact problem he identified: establishing a denomination that actually works for everyday people.

**The Cognitive Barrier of 2 Quadrillion**

The free market naturally gravitates toward a dual-asset standard to minimize cognitive friction. While Bitcoin protects purchasing power, the Satoshi (Sat) fails as an intuitive unit of account for the working class.

Observe the math when global wealth (roughly $120 Trillion) is fully absorbed into the network:

 **$120 Trillion ÷ 2 Quadrillion Sats = $0.06 per Sat.**

Under this framework, a basic $14 toy costs roughly 233 Sats (or 0.00000233 BTC). A child cannot conceptualize 233, nor can they grasp microscopic decimals. If children in poverty cannot easily count their savings, they cannot develop a low time preference. They will inevitably fall back into the cognitive trap of fiat.

Furthermore, expecting the global population to measure their daily survival against a 2 quadrillion supply cap is a fundamental design flaw. A "quadrillion" is a number so massive and abstract that it breaks human comprehension. It belongs to the realm of theoretical physics and academic elites, not the working class. It creates immediate mental fatigue, making prices harder to read, remember, and communicate.

**The Nah•Sovereign•Diamond Solution**

We must downsize the cognitive framework so absolute scarcity becomes legible to the masses. The human brain is already accustomed to the scale of trillions in modern economics. By shifting the supply cap from an incomprehensible quadrillion to a manageable 85.3 trillion, the math aligns perfectly with human intuition.

 **$120 Trillion ÷ 85.3 Trillion Nahs = ~$1.40 per Nah.**

Another kitten tried to follow us home last night.
items.text:
Last night, while walking home with my family (my husband and daughter), a kitten appeared out of nowhere—it looked to be about a month and a half old, small, white with a little gray tail. It walked between our feet, making sounds and looking up at us as it followed; it was surely hungry. It broke my heart not to be able to take it home to give it food and shelter. The only solution I could think of was to go look for it today and take it to the cat shelter; at least I know there are makeshift little houses there where it can take cover from the rain, and I can bring it food regularly. If it stays here, it runs the risk of being eaten by a larger animal or getting run over. I don't know why, but I was left with a sense of responsibility toward that cat; I felt bad about leaving it behind.

items.title: Is starting another coin the best way to fix Bitcoin?
items.text:
Forgive my clickbait title, but in setting up this week's Bitdev's list I came across this delving post about "fixing" Bitcoin's security budget via tail emissions and other convoluted mechanics. I don't really care about that. 

I found this [response](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/addressing-the-diminishing-block-subsidy/2640/11) from Pieter Wuille (aka sipa) thought-provoking:

![](https://m.stacker.news/156952)

We've recently experienced this dynamic: a group of Bitcoiners were very dissatisfied with the fact that arbitrary data was being embedded in Bitcoin blocks and they thought that the rules should be changed to attempt to limit such data. We spent a fiery couple years arguing about the details of changing Bitcoin, but in the end they ended up with a new coin. Kinda wish they had just done that from the beginning.

![](https://m.stacker.news/156955)

Bitcoin has some problems. Indeed, it would be rather startling if it was the case that Satoshi got everything right right off the bat. The history of Bitcoin is littered with the scorch marks of people who wanted it to change in a certain way and who ended up leaving to start their own thing. 

This leads me to wonder, if, instead of trying to get Bitcoin to adopt any given change, 

# Maybe the best way to improve bitcoin is to launch a new coin

Of course, as we are seeing with bcashjr, it's not quite so simple as that. There is a quality of being Bitcoin that comes from the fact that it was first. I've heard people talk about this like the immaculate conception. Their theology is horrible, but the common sense point comes across: Bitcoin's launch may have been a bit of a perfect storm. 

And this is where I wonder if Wuille isn't wrong: it's easy enough to tell someone to go try it on a new coin, but I tihnk it's very likely that even some hypothetical coin that is better than BTC will fail simply because the dynamics of launching a new coin.

I know that there was a time when Bitcoin Maximalism meant that all the things will be done on Bitcoin and that the standard way of viewing the shitcoins was that many of them were testing out things that might eventually come to bitcoin (eg Mimble Wimble on Litecoin), so maybe Wuille is just saying what has always been said. 

I do love the idea of the market always being the answer, and when I think about the current process by which we attempt to change bitcoin, it strikes me that the market is not really involved at all. I would much rather have Covenant Coin compete in the market with BTC to see how much market participants value each coin.

Watching the bcashjr launch -- while humorous and highly entertaining -- has also given me pause: go launch your own coin is maybe not such a realistic suggestion as might be assumed.

items.title: Rocket Mass Heater - Extremely efficient wood heater
items.text:
We can heat our well insulated 900sqft of living space to 65-70°f using around 2 cords of wood each year with our Rocket Mass Heater. We typically wake up to 65°f and burn a fire in the morning and another fire in the evening. A "J" tube burn chamber covered by a 55gal barrel creates radiant heat as well as a thermal pump which forces exhaust gasses horizontally though ducting in a large box filled with pea gravel. The gravel extracts most of the heat from the exhaust radiating it out slowly after the fire burns out. By the time the exhaust reaches the chimney it's 120-200°f down from 300-500°f at the barrel. The combustion is nearly total so very little smoke is exhausted and maximum BTUs are used to heat the space. Built with materials found at most big box hardware stores Rocket Mass Heaters are cheap to build, easy to source, and incredibly efficient. It is the favorite contraption I've built on the homestead. 
![](https://i.imgur.com/K6gcMsJ.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/dZW4Pmi.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/LZUbQ5C.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/fw7spU4.jpeg)
![](https://i.imgur.com/EV85lDZ.jpeg)

Here's a note I wrote about our Rocket mass heater a few years ago to provide some more details on how amazing these heaters are:

Now that transaction fee storm has passed I'm back to heating my living space primarily with wood in a rocket mass heater instead of Asics.
![](https://v.nostr.build/Ee2K.mp4)
Wood is burned in the small firebox and heat radiates from the barrel warming the space quickly while the fire burns.
https://i.nostr.build/2xaq.jpg
As the exhaust gasses make their way to the chimney, they pass through ductwork in a plywood box filled with pea gravel. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/0g92.jpg)
The majority of the heat from the exhaust is transfered to the gravel before exiting up the chimney. By the time the gases exit the box, they are cool enough for me to put my hand on the chimney pipe. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/An5E.jpg)
After the fire burns out, the heat absorbed by the pea gravel slowly radiates out into the living space until the next fire is burned and the gravel is recharged with heat once again. I built this rocket mass heater for a fraction of the cost of a wood burning insert, with no special tools, materials, or skills.
![](https://i.nostr.build/DZBa.jpg)
It has been an unusually warm November and December here at the homestead. Normally we have to start burning wood in the rocket mass heater early November to stay comfortable but this year, the bitcoin mining dehydrator was enough to stay warm and do some food preservation simultaneously. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/2Dw8.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/479W.jpg)
Transaction fees started climbing and I was shocked to see the most efficient miner I had approaching break even at my electric rate.
![](https://i.nostr.build/2vyP.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/GZ2J.jpg)
I didn't have the circuit to run it wired yet but this bump in fees was the motivation I needed to get the miner hashing. Coincidentally, the weather also started to get colder finally so getting the miner up and running was a win/win. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/nxkq.jpg)
It successfully kept us and our guests warm through the holidays, even earning some Bitcoin beyond the cost of power at times, all while allowing us to save our firewood. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/XdWL.jpg)
We did have to fire up the rocket mass heater a handful of times, but so far we've burned less than half the amount of wood compared to previous years. This is thanks to the combination of the warm weather, and high transaction fees allowing us to stay warm with heavily subsidized electric heat. 
![](https://i.nostr.build/K2xl.jpg)
This might be the first winter we make it through with wood leftover for the next year, typically I'm scrounging for the last couple weeks.

items.title: [Read-Along] The Odyssey (W.H.D Rouse transl.), Remarks
items.text:
# Some thoughts

Here I am proposing doing something maybe a little juvenile, so you are free to be all growed up and just observe. 

Here is also my attempt at changing @denlillaapan 's mind about stories. Although I know he's reviewed fiction here, I am not convinced he has done so for any reason other than he thought it might be a good way to seduce me to zap his posts in the territory. 

That aside, my other-half--who works arguably harder than I do--has been having trouble sleeping, so I have offered to read to her a bedtime story so that she stays away from her screen.  We picked the Odyssey and we have just finished Book 1. So far, the results have been positive.

# The translation

Selected edition: *[The Odyssey, Homed. Translated by W.H.D. Rouse.](https*://a.co/d/08xXX1xi)*

After toying with the idea of not watching the film, and reading the poem instead, I came across the translation of [W.H.D Rouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._H._D._Rouse), which--to me--strikes a fair balance in using lay-person friendly language while, at the same time, is uncontroversial in its treatment of the classical ethics that readers often look for in the poem. 

The Odyssey, in it's heyday, wouldn't have been thought of as a 'book' per se, but a poetic performance. Kind of like how you watch Netflix before you doze off to sleep, except, to my knowledge, there was no internet in the classical period of Greek history. Bards performed sections of this epic poem, which had to be committed to memory, for every day folk like you and me. This oral tradition of the poem means that it should be made accessible to as many people as possible, which I think this translation is. 

# A read-along

I have chosen to call it a read-along, because you can contribute as well as just observe and learn about the poem. It will not follow book-club logic. There is no schedule. Anyone can contribute at any time. Just get a copy, read a chapter (preferably without skipping ahead), and then post your summary. 

A note on pacing: my wife and I do not have a long attention span, may have missed a day here and there, and so it took us a week to get through book 1 (11 pages). I think those who wish to read along will find this pace amenable. 
# Read-along summary suggestions  

As I do this, I may have other ideas, but for each "Book" I am thinking the following would be nice to have: 

- a short summary of the story 
- a key character list (including gods, humans, giants, etc.)
- key places mentioned 
- some thoughts/questions

If you do participate, I may catalogue it in a pinned post on ~the_stacker_muse territory. In that case, I will use the following naming convention: 

> [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, <Book Number>

That way at the end we'll have a neat looking list of posts to compile and passers-by can peruse and learn about the epic poem. 

Also, please feel free to cross-post in ~BooksAndArticles (I hear there are some pretty juicy rewards sloshing around over there). 

# Join me 

If you are interested and would like to get your hands on a copy, you have a few days before I update you on Book 1. 

So what are you waiting for, get off your damn government-surveilling, blue-light radiating, endocrine-disrupting smartphones and join me as I read the greatest story ever told.

items.title: Slowly Exiting the Fiat World with Bitcoin e-SIM
items.text:
Recently, I noticed my current SIM card subscription is about to expire, so I checked how much the new subscription will cost. The SIM provider has jacked up the price over the years in the name of giving you MORE internet data, which I barely use. I don't really need 50 GB each month or 2000 mins for calls. *It's really important to know what you actually need, because the fiat world loves to package things you don't need.* So I was thinking maybe switch to prepaid, pay-as-I-go, and I had to call the call center *three* times to get it done. **Only after going through things like this do you really appreciate how much better the experience is with Bitcoin e-SIM services.**

I would like to share the current Bitcoin e-SIM options (mainly for internet and receiving messages) and my experience here.

***

### [**Silent link**](https://silent.link)

No KYC, no email needed. I have been using Silent Link for at least two years, and I've traveled to different countries with it. You are literally able to access the local internet the second you land, which is really handy for travelers!

Another bonus: even in places where one local provider is weak, you can manually switch to another, which basically means you can choose the provider whenever instead of locking into one like in the fiat world.

**Pricing**: $9 for data only, with a $5 initial balance.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155973)

The paying experience is great. Onchain and LN payment available. It redirects to a unique link with a QR code after you pay, then you just scan it with your phone, super easy. **Don't forget to bookmark the unique link for later top-ups.** Top-up is super simple too: just go back to the unique link you bookmarked, create an invoice, and pay.

To check how much money is left, dial \*187#.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155974)

Silent Link also offers number rental (US numbers only). I tried that too, but the number I got couldn't register for some apps, so I stopped using it.

***

### [**Nadanada**](https://nadanada.me/)

No KYC, no email needed. Nadanada has more services than Silent Link, including VPN, e-SIM, disposable numbers, and number rental; I tested the 3-month rental number, and I quite liked the overall experience, especially the part that you don't need to download another App so to receive messages, all you need is simply log back in to the link, which is super cool!

**Pricing**

3-month UK rental number: $12; 12-month UK rental number: $44.

![](https://m.stacker.news/155975)

It also redirects to a unique link after payment, don't forget to bookmark it for renew or to receive messages.

I think Nadanada is especially good for business. Don't use Google Voice or anything like that, because they would take the number back for no reason. One more detail to share is **that you need to verify the rental number's cleanliness before renting it long-term.** For example, I got two numbers from Nadanada; one can register for most apps I tested, but the other had trouble with one app.

Another issue I've found so far is that **once the rental period expires, you can't renew the same number anymore, and all your message history is gone too**, which isn't good if you want to use it for something important. You can definitely rent it for one year or longer and even set a remind email, but do keep that in mind.

*I have a suggestion: how about giving people a grace period to renew the same number after it expires? Maybe even an option to download the message history.* @nadanada_me

***

### **The Art of Slowly Exiting the Fiat World**

I'm aware that a local SIM is necessary for local delivery and any Gov-related things, but it's better to limit its use; for example, avoid using it to register any of your online profiles.

My current setup is a prepaid local SIM, Silent Link for internet, and Nadanada for sites that need a verification code. The best part about these Bitcoin e-SIMs is that you pay for what you actually use, and even better: **you might develop a better habit of using your phone less when you're out!**

Less screen time, less internet use, spend less money (save more sats), and spend more time in real life with people around you, which sounds quite a good deal! I've started taking a notebook with me now. Since I am learning a new language, I can spend more time learning instead of checking what's going on on the internet.

***

### **Disclosures**

I won't get paid or anything for recommending them, I just enjoy finding tools that make my life easier, and happy to share my experience. **After you try how things work with Bitcoin, you simply CAN'T go back to fiat companies.** Since a few people have asked previously, "Will you use Bitcoin as your everyday money?" It actually starts with small things like this.

Once you taste the simplicity and peace of mind compared with fiat companies, you will slowly try to find alternatives to exit the fiat world. Even better, you learn how to create it yourself if you can't find it.

Enjoy! ⚡️

items.title: Latest Strikes #36 & #37 - Augst 31st - September 13th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your (lately bi-) weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. As in the past few issues, this edition is heavily focused on software security releases. We've got releases from all major implementations to cover, exploits, and more.

![](https://m.stacker.news/157252)

## rust-lightning Release & Candidate

[https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1) of [rust-lightning](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning) was released 2 weeks ago, improving on splicing, Bolt12 and more. A few personal picks:

* pending splices can now be RBF'd, and it is now possible to splice funds in and out in a single transaction;
* Bolt12 payments can now receive arbitrary metadata, and support for Bolt12 [Payer Proofs](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-21#experimental-bolt12-payer-proofs-in-core-lightning) was added;
* anchor channels can now drop the requirement for a remote (trusted) party to hold a reserve in the channel, which is especially useful in the LSP context as it allows the user to spend their whole balance.

Note that this release brings some incompatibilities. Notably:

* v0.3-rc1 is a breaking change for Bolt11 invoices carrying metadata, because now the invoice's secret commits to those. Existing metadata-bearing invoices will be invalidated, and invoices generated under v0.3-rc1 would be invalidated by a downgrade;
* outbound payments still awaiting a Bolt12 invoice response won't complete across the upgrade;
* Bolt12 refunds issued before the update will not be claimable after updating.

See the full [backwards compatibility report](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.3-rc1#user-content-backwards-compatibility) before upgrading.

A week later, the maintenance release [0.2.6](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/releases/tag/v0.2.6) was also released, bringing bug and security fixes to the stable 0.2 line:

* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4983) to a bug that could lead to a node crashing on restart in some circumstances. When a channel is closed while it has not seen any activity and doesn't hold any funds for the node, the node archives the monitoring of this channel right away, since there's nothing else to do about it. However, this early archiving could lead to a state where the `ChannelManager` component still holds an entry for this channel, but with no corresponding monitoring, leading to a crash on restart (the manager refuses to deserialize);
* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4905) in rust-lightning's splice negotiation protocol, where a counterparty initiating a splice could inflate their apparent contribution to the fee[^1], passing checks while actually paying a lower fee than agreed. Crucially, this lowers the effective transaction fee, potentially increasing confirmation time, while letting the initiator pocket the difference in their own output;
* a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4982) to another bug where the `ChannelManager` refuses to deserialize on restart, this time caused by a bogus HTLC (immediately rejected but leaving an empty entry) followed by a valid and successfully forwarded HTLC with the same hash. This can be triggered remotely by anyone routing a payment through your node, and leads to the same failure on restart as the above "early channel archiving" bug.

Outside of these releases, a [fix](https://git.rust-bitcoin.org/lightningdevkit/rust-lightning/pulls/4954) was also merged for a stale buffer bug that could lead to a channel force close after a splice, if the peers disconnect at a specific point during the splice protocol. This bug was found through fuzzing.

## Core Lightning Embargo Ending & Heads Up

There have been [reports](https://x.com/evankaloudis/status/2099582283409674260) early this week of users getting funds [stolen](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/issues/9498) on (even the latest version of) Core Lightning when using the dual-funding feature. Yesterday, Core Lightning's official X account issued a [Security Advisory](https://x.com/Core_LN/status/2099927317107839188), urging operators to disable all [experimental features](https://docs.corelightning.org/reference/lightningd-config#experimental-options) immediately while investigations continue. Such experimental features include dual-funding, some LSP-related features, and more. While incredibly wide, this advice appears to confirm the substantiality of the above reports, so Core Lightning operators should exercise extreme caution. When possible, the `--offline` flag remains an [option](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#:~:text=Restart%20in%20%E2%80%9Coffline%E2%80%9D%20mode%2E) to stop peer traffic while still watching the chain.

On another note, the embargo on the latest Core Lightning [release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#core-lightning-release) was lifted last Friday (September 11th), meaning we now have access to the source code for this [release](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/releases/tag/v26.06.7). If you have not yet done so, I strongly encourage you to update to this latest version (v26.06.7) of Core Lightning.

An analysis of the [changelog](https://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning/compare/v26.06.6...v26.06.7) shows a few predominant topics. While the summary below is definitely not exhaustive, it covers some of the fixes that appear especially important to me.

### Revoked Commitment Disguised As Mutual Close (scaryyyy)

When a peer opens a channel with no upfront shutdown script, they can specify this script later, at close time. It was possible for an attacker to cause a Core Lightning node to mis-classify a force close with a revoked commitment as a mutual close, by using the `to_local` script of a past commitment as the shutdown script. Failing to detect the force close, the CLN node would not broadcast a justice transaction, allowing the peer to steal funds.

### On-chain Preimage vs. Unfinished Failure

Given 2 HTLCs with the same payment hash, a peer can fulfill one and fail the other, stop before either removal is final (old state revoked), and claim both HTLCs on-chain with the preimage. In that case, the specification adequately states that the preimage path wins, but Core Lightning would skip the "pending fail" HTLC. For a routing node, this could lead to loss of funds, since the outgoing HTLC is settled on-chain but the incoming one is never settled and eventually times out.

### On-chain Feerate Fixes

As we all know, Lightning remains strongly anchored to on-chain Bitcoin. While this is what confers Lightning its very strong self-custodial guarantees, it also comes with the drawback of exposing Lightning nodes to a range of bugs and attacks stemming from badly managed on-chain feerates.

* In mutual closes, a CLN node could apparently be "talked into" paying a higher feerate than it would have under a unilateral close. The unilateral close feerate, fed from the estimator with current on-chain conditions, now acts as an upper bound for the negotiation of the mutual close feerate;
* In splicing and dual-funding, a CLN node would accept any feerate from the peer, even if outside of the node's boundaries, which weren't properly piped there. A counterparty could therefore have the CLN node store an absurdly high feerate, or on the other side agree to a feerate as low as 0 (for dual-funding, splicing already has a lower bound), causing untimely confirmation or no valid RBF path. In the case of Core Lightning accepting absurdly high feerates in splicing/dual-funding, this could render RBF impossible (due to Bolt 2 ["25/24 rule"](https://github.com/lightning/bolts/blob/master/02-peer-protocol.md#rationale-5)), and could even in some cases lead to a node-wide crash loop on startup due to a u32 overflow.

### Remote DoS Fixes

Speaking of crashes, this security release also addresses a number of remotely triggerable DoS vectors, on top of the "feerate poisoning" one mentioned above.

* a node hostname crafted to be over 248 bytes, advertised through gossip, could crash the `connectd` subdaemon when attempting to connect to the corresponding node, crashing the whole node;
* a specifically crafted onion message could crash the offers plugin, resulting in a wider crash of the whole node;
* peers could have as many simultaneous dual-funded (v2) channel openings in progress as they wanted, which could exhaust a Core Lightning node's resources with a very high number of in-flight channel openings;
* an especially large unauthenticated request to a `clnrest` endpoint with a bad rune would crash the node with a segfault. This of course only affects nodes running clnrest, with the corresponding port open;
* some deeply nested JSON could exhaust the C stack and crash the process parsing the offending JSON. For example, `commando` parses peer-supplied JSON before checking the rune, so any connected peer could crash the plugin and the node.

## LND Release

Version [0.21.3](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/releases/tag/v0.21.3-beta) of LND is out, identical to the release candidate we covered [2 weeks ago](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-34-35#lnd-releases). On top of what we already covered there, notable changes are:

* the fix to a [bug](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/10782) that could lead channels to end up in a limbo state if during a mutual close negotiation a peer disconnected before the close transaction was finalized;
* the [fix](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/10869) to a bug where the channel counterparty spending an HTLC output could be treated as the node's own success transaction, passing a non-existent output to the sweeper, potentially poisoning sweep batches[^2];
* a new [RPC](https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lnd/pull/11065) enabling the creation of on-chain sub-wallets with spending capabilities inside the same node, allowing a single wallet to be split into smaller pockets that each control their own outputs. This new feature is experimental, and funds held in these sub-wallets cannot be recovered with only the seed phrase.

## Eclair Release

I'd like to mention *en passant* that ACINQ published a security [release](https://github.com/ACINQ/eclair/releases/tag/v0.14.3) for Eclair last Monday. Since this new version was released only 2 days ago, it belongs to next week's newsletter, but I wanted to let you know so you can update as soon as possible. Per ACINQ's release notes, the developers "highly recommend upgrading, as some of these issues can be exploited by malicious nodes".

## Electrum Release

Version [4.8.2](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/blob/master/RELEASE-NOTES#:~:text=Release%204.8.2%20(September%2011%2C%202026)%20(security%20update)) of the Electrum wallet was released, and it's a security release. It includes several Lightning-related fixes, notably:

* payments sent are [no longer](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/pull/10962) marked as failed when the receiver can still claim them because there are still some pending HTLCs;
* multiple fixes to payment forwarding, which is still experimental in Electrum;
* for some wallets (those using non-deterministic Lightning keys and anchor channels), the channel backup missed some critical key material, making recovery of funds in Lightning channels impossible because they lacked the key to sweep the `to_remote` output after the peer force-closed the channel. This is now [fixed](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/pull/10852).

## Alby Hub Vulnerability For Old Versions

A [vulnerability](https://x.com/getAlby/status/2097574956049498150) affecting old versions (more than a year!) of Alby Hub appear to have been exploited in the wild. We don't have the full details yet, but it seems the vulnerability could "allow an attacker who could reach the Hub's management API to gain unauthorized access and send funds", if the Hub is publicly accessible from the internet.

Please, in the name of Satoshi, update your software, especially if it holds keys to Bitcoin funds. The affected versions here are v1.7.0 to v1.18.5 (prior to August 2025), and version 1.19.0 (August 2025) or newer are unaffected.

## Swiss Bitcoin Pay Vulnerability & Hack

While doing a generalized [review](https://kek.lol/research/appstore-wallets/) of Bitcoin wallets available on app stores, [BlueWallet](https://bluewallet.io/) CTO Igor (aka overtorment) found a critical vulnerability in [Swiss Bitcoin Pay](https://swiss-bitcoin-pay.ch/) (SBP), an app that lets merchants receive on-chain and Lightning payments without having to manage a node. On-chain payments are directly sent to the merchant's wallet in self-custody, and Lightning payments are sent to SBP's Lightning node and automatically withdrawn to the merchant's on-chain wallet periodically (e.g. every 24 hours). However, as Igor found, the app posted the full BIP39 mnemonic to its API when a user completed wallet signup/login. This has since been [fixed](https://github.com/SwissBitcoinPay/app/commit/1a23cb2e811f584639bdfe01d78765705bdc2398), but the extent to which user seeds were exposed remains unclear. If you used SBP before, it is strongly advised to remove funds from the wallet and create a new one.

Shortly after the finding, SBP's systems were also [breached](https://x.com/SwissBitcoinPay/status/2099473448162488618), potentially (personal opinion here!) by an actor looking to access the mnemonics if those were stored or logged on SBP's servers. According to SBP's communication, user funds are safe (which I believe includes Lightning funds that were pending automatic dispatch), and "any amounts owed to users will be fully returned". However, attackers "may have accessed customer email addresses, Bitcoin addresses and IBANs, transaction history, and hashed passwords" and it is "not yet clear whether any other information was accessed".

So yeah, this is pretty bad. Once again, if you have funds on an SBP wallet, I encourage you to move them to a new wallet asap.

## Zeus Release

Zeus [v13.2.1](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.1) was released with, you guessed it, its load of security fixes. Especially worth noting are:

* the [bump](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4489) of the pinned LDK version used in Zeus (for the LDK embedded node) from a December 2025 snapshot to the 0.2 release branch head (v0.2.5). This therefore brings to Zeus all the LDK security fixes released up to v0.2.5 of rust-lightning;
* a [fix](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4362) to a bug (and potential vulnerability) whereby a user could review a given invoice A and end up paying a different invoice B when clicking "Pay". This could happen when a new invoice (B) was pushed to the wallet while the user had begun reviewing the first invoice (A). While the user initially reviewed invoice A, their validation would trigger the payment of invoice B. This second invoice could have been received in the wallet through any of the available vectors, including "the universal input router for QR, clipboard, deep links, and NFC";
* when paying an LNURL Pay URL or a Lightning Address, Zeus didn't check that the invoice's description hash matched the metadata supplied by the LNURL server, which could allow a malicious server to display "benign identity metadata" (e.g. what the Zeus user expects for this payment) while the actual invoice paid by the wallet "commits to an unrelated description hash \[or requests] an arbitrary amount". This is now [fixed](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4374).

## Zaprite

Zaprite [revealed](https://x.com/parkeralewis/status/2095534387844497702) the [Zaprite P2P App](https://zapritep2p.com/), with the goal of seamlessly coordinating payments between end users and across wallets. Reminiscent of Zaprite's main merchant payment facilitator [product](https://zaprite.com), users begin by connecting one or many of the supported wallets in the app. Someone wishing to pay them can then find them through the app (by username or phone number), pick which wallet they want to send from, and on the receiver's side Zaprite P2P will automatically route the payment to one of the connected wallets[^3]. Instead of the sender initiating the payment, the receiver can also create a payment request, where they can specify their preferred wallet for reception. If the sender doesn't have the app, a Zaprite P2P link allows them to pay nonetheless, directly to the receiver's wallet.

***

That's it for the last 2 weeks. As always, thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: They achieve that by disguising the channel's current funding output as one of their own UTXOs added as input to the splicing transaction. The receiving node therefore treats the funds in the UTXO as belonging exclusively to the attacker, whereas they're actually shared funds in the channel.

[^2]: Because the underlying Bitcoin node rejects the sweep as invalid, since it tries to spend a non-existent output.

[^3]: There are many ways to handle this, but I guess an algorithm trying to minimize costs and maximize reliability will try to match the sender's wallet if the receiver also has it; and otherwise select the best next wallet on the receiver's side.

items.title: Using Bitcoin Miners to Make Maple Syrup
items.text:
Immersion mining with canola oil to concentrate maple sap more quickly
![](https://v.nostr.build/n997.mp4)
I'm using a single S9 hash board immersed in canola oil to heat maple sap to increase the effectiveness of the reverse osmosis sap concentration system.
![](https://i.nostr.build/okkw.jpg)
The weather conditions this season have caused the maple sap to be cold and stay cold which drastically slows down the ability of the RO system to filter water out of it. I ran into a bottle neck where there is more sap than I can keep up with concentrating so I needed to come up with something quickly!
![](https://i.nostr.build/B33D.jpg)
Ideally if the temperature of the sap is 77°f the filter will operate most effectively without damaging the RO membrane. Of course, my mind immediately turned to Bitcoin mining for the heating solution. What I came up with was an immersion system using the homebrew equipment I already had to heat the sap just before it entered the RO. This would allow the majority of the sap to stay cool keeping it from spoiling and still remove the most water possible.
![](https://i.nostr.build/e0Jz.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/aokZ.jpg)
The only thing I didn't have for the immersion system was the dielectric fluid. I had no idea where to find the proper fluid nor did it make sense to pay the high cost for it. The application for this system is very specific and I will only need it until April. I had been joking about using canola oil as dielectric fluid for almost a year but for this situation it seemed like the perfect fit. Canola oil is 70% cheaper than bitcool before shipping and was immediately available!
![](https://i.nostr.build/rDv2.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/J3qq.jpg)
Amazingly, I put everything together and it worked very well without major adjustments. I tip-toed the voltage and frequency of the single S9 hashboard up slowly to find the right balance in temperatures between the two fluid loops. Ultimately, I ended up with an overclocked board drawing over 600w! By the time I got the system setup and dialed in I was already half way through concentrating this collection of sap. The next collection will offer more concrete data on what this system is capable of. For now, even with the worst S9 board I have, I'm getting a 15% rebate on the total power usage of the whole process and it's definitely concentrating sap more quickly. All for ~$10 of canola oil... 👀

items.title: Trip Report: Paris
items.text:
Paris is known for its food and savoir vivre, the art of living your life. It comes as no surprise that the merchants I found accepting Bitcoin in Paris are all serving foods and drinks, and so this trip report is almost more of a food review than a Bitcoin review.

🧆In the hip 18th arrondissement lies Chez Ginette, a fairly typical cafe with its seats facing the trottoir, so Parisians can watch each other. The menu offers all the classic dishes you would expect from a place like this, but somehow lacks a theme or specialization. I order the greatest classic there is, the steak tartare. It comes préparé, meaning the raw egg is mixed in. It's definitely of high quality and I'm also happy about the pommes frites on the side. There is a "Bitcoin Lightning payments accepted" sticker on the door, and as I ask to pay with Bitcoin the waiter does not hesitate, although it takes him a while to get his colleague to come over with an orange point of sale terminal running the Swiss Bitcoin Pay app, built on BTCPay. The payment goes through almost instantly.

🍸Le Greffulhe is another cafe close to the opera and a high-end fashion district. As I arrive I mistake a man standing by the entrance for staff and ask him about Bitcoin paymnets. He says he would be surprised if they did, and indeed he is after we go inside together to ask the cashier. The cafe belongs to the same category as Chez Ginette, but the atmosphere feels very different, and although they do serve food, I never got the chance to try it during my two visits. Instead I had Aperol Spritz and Campari Soda, and payments went smoothly to the mobile phone of the cashier, also running Swiss Bitcoin Pay.

🍺Undoubtedly the heart of the Paris Bitcoin community is N'importe Quoi near Les Halles, somewhat in the geographical center of the city. The dive bar has the kind of anarchic and old-school feminist feel of a place that you almost expect to be taking Bitcoin. I'm here quite early and all by myself, and at first the bar tender denies my Bitcoin payment, saying "usually we do." Eventually she shows mercy with me and digs up the phone that has fallen somewhere behind the cash register, presumably only kept for the sole purpose of processing Bitcoin payments. The bar also uses Swiss Bitcoin Pay, and I'm quite pleased with how fast I can find a route to their node, and how I never paid more than 0.09% in fees, just a few sats.

🍝The Italian restaurant Costa d'Amalfi greets visitors with a warning: No Pizza. Connoisseurs will recognize this as a sign of quality, and indeed the family-run trattoria is exactly the kind of place you typically see accepting Bitcoin in Italy. Everything is well curated, the menu is short and specializes in one thing: truffle dishes. The owner comes over to talk to me about Bitcoin, telling me stories of his family and his Bitcoin story. He also uses the now familiar Swiss Bitcoin Pay and is quite happy with it.

🥮Located near Volontaires, an hommage to the volunteer soldiers of the French Revolution, is one of the areas of Paris known for their contemporary bohème lifestyle. Le Drapeau de la Fidélité fits it perfectly with its nondescript facade and carefully curated interior. There are plenty of books that make the restaurant feel more like a library, and they appear to have actually been read frequently. There are antiques, paintings, signed letters and a banner proclaiming a "Universal Humanist Capitalist Society" that I cannot find any other information about. The owner, a well-dressed older Vietnamese gentleman appears to run the tiny restaurant with its maybe 12 seats together with his son. The menu is short and the dishes simple and affordable. I order the porc caramélisé and pay a round 18,000 satoshi. The owner seems quite pleased with me paying with Bitcoin, which is always a great feeling when spending it. He uses Cake wallet, but doesn't know how to set an amount for his invoices. Also, his wallet is priced in USD, meaning I have to look up the rate on my end. As far as routing fees go, it's by far my most expensive payment at 0.3%.

🍷Near the Gare d'Austerlitz I visit La Brasserie L'Audièrnes. The area seems to be very popular with students, and everyone at the bar seems to be talking about AI, with many conversations in English. I order my drink at the bar and pay right away, but the cashier is hesitant to show me his wallet, and instead asks his colleague over. We navigate through the interface of some unfamiliar crypto wallet, and all we can find is an onchain address, which I pay to reluctantly.

I'm quite happy with my visit to Paris and especially the Bitcoin places that I found. I love the opportunity to find some random or hidden gems in the city that I would have never been able to visit if it weren't for Bitcoin. I love talking to the staff and the owners, there is always something to learn, and sometimes to teach, about how people are using Bitcoin. I also went to six other places, four of which were closed, and two of which no longer accept Bitcoin. At one of these places, the doors and cash register covered in Bitcoin stickers, I was practically laughed at for asking to pay with Bitcoin, before being asked to pay one Bitcoin to buy everyone a round. Finally one reason to implement BIP 177.
